questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of secondary data?

options.text: Measuring the heights of students in your class
Conducting a survey of your neighbours
Using census data from a government website
Counting cars in a car park

questions.explanation: Secondary data is data that has already been collected by someone else. Census data from a government website is a classic example.

questions.stem: A company has 240 men and 160 women. A stratified sample of 40 is needed. How many women should be selected?
A student asks: 'Don't you agree the school canteen is terrible?' This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The phrasing 'Don't you agree...' pushes the respondent toward a particular answer, making it a leading (biased) question.

questions.stem: In random sampling, every member of the population has:

options.text: A zero chance of being selected
A chance proportional to their age
A guaranteed place in the sample
An equal chance of being selected

questions.explanation: In random sampling, every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.

questions.stem: For systematic sampling from a population of 900 with a sample of 30, you would select every:
questions.explanation: The sampling interval $k = \frac{900}{30} = 30$. You select every 30th person from an ordered list.

options.text: Certain groups are systematically over- or under-represented
It is taken from the whole population

questions.explanation: A sample is biased when it systematically favours certain groups, making it unrepresentative of the whole population.

questions.stem: Which sampling method divides the population into groups and selects proportionally from each?
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into strata (groups) and selects from each group in proportion to its size.
